newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook--Churning copper spreads in focus.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook--Churning copper spreads in focus.

text.p: All eyes in the metals market this week will be on copper spreads as nervous players wait for shorts to cover exposed positions after a squeeze hit the market last week, analysts said.
The benchmark cash/threes spread climbed to a $210 backwardation last week, up from about $30 the previous week.
Tightness is mainly centred from late April to mid-May and the first tight date is due to be traded later on Monday.

The cash/day spread had the potential to surge to the LME-imposed limit of one percent of the previous day's cash settlement before the game was over, but it was impossible to say how much without knowing the size of the shorts' positions, analysts said.
"It's very hard to predict how it's all going to turn out," said analyst Jim Lennon of broker Macquarie Equities. "Our feeling is the market will edge higher and then fizzle out again."
In late January, the cash/threes backwardation flipped to a $300 backwardation, but it deflated fairly quickly as lending came on to the market and metal was delivered into LME warehouses.

"Some people are looking for a move as high as $300 but bearing in mind the speed of recent gains, this could be a little hopeful," said broker GNI in a commentary on Friday. "Chart gap resistance between $230 and $245 has to be breached first."
In early pre-market trade on Monday, the benchmark spread was indicated at a $205/$210 backwardation, while three months was quoted just above $2,400.
Three months prices gained about $100 last week as the squeeze took hold and a series of production problems surfaced.

The market will be keeping track of news from Escondida, where a strike continues among about 17 percent of the 2,000-strong workforce. A trade union official said last week the mine had run out of concentrates but mine officials declined to comment.

Other labour problems and production glitches were keeping the pot boiling while there was word that Chinese buyers were back in the market, even if their activity so far was only modest, Lennon said.
"They may have used up the stocks they built up late last year," he added.
The stocks situation will be closely watched, since the backwardation is likely to suck metal into warehouses.
Last week LME inventories fell by 7,275 tonnes to 145,200 tonnes.
The other metals were more in the background, having ticked higher with copper but failing to show any strong impetus on their own.
Three month aluminium toyed with the $1,600 level last week, finishing on Friday positively at $1,613, a touch above the 30-day moving average.
Early on Monday, the market pushed to $1,632.
